style: |
  /*
   * Percona look, after the Percona Live 2026 Amsterdam deck: charcoal #282727,

  @font-face { font-family: 'Poppins'; font-weight: 300; font-display: block; src: url(data:font/woff2;base64,) format('woff2'); }
  @font-face { font-family: 'Poppins'; font-weight: 600; font-display: block; src: url(data:font/woff2;base64,) format('woff2'); }

  :root {

    --white: #ffffff;
    --violet: #653df4;
    --lime: #f6fe54;
    --dim: #8a8888;

    padding: 96px 230px 120px 102px;
  }

  section.section {

  section::before {

  section.dark::after, section.section::after { bottom: 80px; }

  ul { margin: 0; padding: 0; list-style: none; }

  section.dark li::before { background: var(--lime); }

  .kicker { font-size: 15px; letter-spacing: 0.08em; text-transform: uppercase; font-weight: 300; color: var(--dim); margin: 0 0 8px; }

  section.title h1 { font-size: 44px; line-height: 1.14; }
  section.title .kicker { color: var(--lime); font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 14px; }
  section.title .speaker { position: absolute; left: 102px; top: 590px; width: 42%; margin: 0; font-size: 18px; line-height: 1.6; opacity: .92; }
  .kclogo { position: absolute; left: 96px; top: 168px; width: 290px; height: 130px; background: var(--kclogo) left top / contain no-repeat; }

  .playmark { width: 44px; height: 48px; margin-top: 30px; background: var(--play) left top / contain no-repeat; }

# Ready. And the app can't connect.

```text
$ kubectl get pg orders -n team-a
NAME     ENDPOINT                      STATUS   POSTGRES   PGBOUNCER   AGE
orders   orders-pgbouncer.team-a.svc   ready    3          1           2m
```

- The operator says `ready`. Whatever your platform puts on top copies it
- The engineer was promised they would never have to look underneath it

<!--
Land it: Ready is a promise, and your platform is the one making it.

- Nothing failed. Every layer tells the truth about what it checks.
-->

---

<!-- _class: dense -->

## What `ready` measures in Percona's PostgreSQL operator

<div class="cols">
<div>

### `getState`, trimmed

```go
if status.PGBouncer.Ready != status.PGBouncer.Size {
	return v2.AppStateInit
}
if status.Postgres.Ready != status.Postgres.Size {
	return v2.AppStateInit
}
return v2.AppStateReady
```

<p class="src">percona/controller/pgcluster/status.go · 52d3dc7</p>

</div>
<div>

### What makes those pods Ready

- Postgres: Patroni's `/readiness`
- PgBouncer: a `// TODO`, no readiness probe
- Nothing logs in as *your* app, so a wrong password, broken pooler auth or an untrusted cert all pass

</div>
</div>

<!--
Land it: the operator's ready is arithmetic over pod counts. Read it before
you copy it up.

- Percona PG operator at 52d3dc7. I work on it, which is why I read it.
-->

---

<!-- _class: dense -->

<style scoped>
table { font-size: 18px; table-layout: fixed; }
th:nth-child(1) { width: 25%; } th:nth-child(2) { width: 47%; } th:nth-child(3) { width: 28%; }
</style>

## Four things the app needs that `ready` never checks

| The app needs | Why it can lag behind `ready` | What the app sees |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Its role and password, in Postgres** | The Secret is written first. Creating the role waits for a writable primary; until then the step returns `nil` | `password authentication failed` |
| **PgBouncer to accept that role** | PgBouncer checks passwords with `pgbouncer.get_auth`, which the operator installs the same way | Logins through the pooler fail |
| **A server cert its CA trusts** | With cert-manager, PgBouncer serves an internal cert until the real one is issued. `TLSSecretsReady` stays `True` | `verify-full` fails, then fixes itself |
| **A network path from its namespace** | NetworkPolicy, mesh and egress rules are platform-owned. No operator can see them | Connection timeout |

Ask the same four questions of every engine you offer.

<!--
Land it: each of these finishes on its own schedule, and none is in the count.

- Row 4 is the one no operator can check.
- Haven't checked MySQL or MongoDB: say "ask", not "they all do this".
-->

---

<!-- _class: dark -->

## Your API has non-human consumers now

- Portals, CLIs, and agent tools all call the same API and read the same field
- An agent waits for Ready, reads the Secret, deploys. Nobody watches the gap
- The failure looks like **its** mistake, so it changes something: rotates the password, recreates the database, or turns off certificate verification
- A rotated password reopens the same gap: the Secret changes first, the SQL follows
- When the gap closes, those changes are still in place

<!--
Land it: a human absorbs the gap by being slow; an agent turns it into an
action.

- Disabling verification is the worst: it stays after the cert arrives.
- Plausible agent behaviour, not observed.
-->

## Close the gap in the platform layer

<div class="cols">
<div>

### Before testing, wait for its inputs

- `observedGeneration` is current, so the operator has at least seen the latest spec
- `status.host` is set, so there is something to dial
- The cert-manager Certificate is Ready, so a TLS failure means something

</div>
<div>

### Then connect the way the app will

- Run it as a Job in the app's namespace, so network policy applies
- Read credentials from the Secret the app mounts, not the operator's original
- Connect with its `pgbouncer-uri` and `sslmode=verify-full`, then run `SELECT 1`
- Set Ready only when that passes

</div>
</div>

<p class="op"><strong>Operators can do part of this.</strong> A condition that logs in as each user through the pooler covers password, pooler and cert. The network path stays with the platform.</p>

<!--
Land it: you do not need to own the operator to own the promise.

- Proposal, not shipped code.
- observedGeneration is necessary, not sufficient: re-test on every
  generation change.
-->

---

<!-- _class: dark -->

## A status an agent can act on

```yaml
status:
  phase: Initializing
  message: waiting for role orders_app in Postgres
  conditions:
  - type: Ready
    status: "False"
    reason: UsersPending
```

- `message` names the step the platform is still waiting for
- Split **wait** from **fix**: a pending reason means poll again, a blocking reason means stop and report
- Each row of the table gets its own reason, the network one included

<!--
Land it: say which kind of not-ready this is.

- Pending: poll with backoff. Blocked: stop and tell a human.
-->

<!-- _class: lead -->

## Measure time to first query, not time to Ready

<div class="cols">
<div>

### Time to Ready

What the platform reports today. Every provisioning dashboard has it.

</div>
<div>

### Time to first query

What the engineer gets. The consumer-side check records it for free.

</div>
</div>

<!--
Land it: put both numbers on the same dashboard.

- No number quoted: I haven't measured it. That is the point of the metric.
-->

---

<!-- _class: lead -->

## Takeaways

1. Read the function that writes your operator's ready, before you copy it up
2. Gate your own Ready on a real connection: from the consumer's namespace, with the consumer's Secret
3. Track time to first query next to time to Ready, and give every not-ready a reason
4. Tell agents what Ready means in your API: test the connection before deploying, wait on a pending reason, and never rotate credentials or relax `sslmode` to fix a connection error

<!--
Land it: point 2.

- If behind, skip the metric slide and say point 3 out loud.
-->
